\section{Finite-Response Mechanics and Effective Coefficients}

\begin{definition}[Finite-response prelimit data]
\label{def:finite_response_prelimit_data}
The slow variable is $x\in\R^m$ and the microscopic variable lies in the
suspension billiard fiber selected by a finite-response parameter
$\Theta(x,p)$.  The mechanical port provides branchwise smooth read-outs:
\begin{equation}
  B(x,p,z),\qquad V(x,p,z),\qquad \Theta(x,p),
\end{equation}
where $B$ is the centered slow drift after subtracting the instantaneous
microcanonical mean and $V$ is the action-density contribution.  These read-outs
are primitive finite-response objects; they are fixed before the effective
Hamiltonian is defined.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Effective coefficients]
\label{def:effective_coefficients}
For each compact jet window, \PaperOne{Primitive spectral and resolvent
theorem}{thm:primitive_spectral_resolvent}, with the continuous-time contour
control from
\PaperOne{Suspension Laplace contour and frequency partition}{lem:suspension_laplace_contour},
gives the zero-mean corrector
\begin{equation}
  \chi_{x,p}=(-\Acal_{\Theta(x,p)}|_{\ker\Pi_{\Theta(x,p)}})^{-1}B(x,p,\cdot).
\end{equation}
The diffusion tensor and Hamiltonian are deterministic pairings in the
anisotropic observable bundle:
\begin{align}
  D(x,p)&=\int_0^\infty
  \langle B(x,p,\cdot),B(x,p,\Phi_{\Theta(x,p)}^t\cdot)\rangle_{\Theta(x,p)}
  \,dt,\\
  H(x,p)&=\langle V(x,p,\cdot)\rangle_{\Theta(x,p)}
  +\hbox{the finite-response work and corrector contributions}.
\end{align}
The HJB operator is
\begin{equation}
  \Hcal(x,p,X)=-\operatorname{tr}(D(x,p)X)-H(x,p).
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Coefficient structure]
\label{prop:coefficient_structure}
On compact jet windows, $D$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite, $H(x,0)=0$,
and $\Hcal$ is affine in the Hessian variable $X$.  The dependence on the
gradient $p$ is inherited from the finite-response port and need not be convex.
All derivatives used below are obtained from
\PaperOne{Smooth deterministic response}{thm:smooth_deterministic_response},
\PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds},
and the finite-response read-outs.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}[Corrector hierarchy and perturbed test]
\label{def:corrector_hierarchy}
Let $\varphi\in C^3$ be a macroscopic test function and set
$p=D\varphi(t,x)$ and $X=D^2\varphi(t,x)$.  The first corrector is the zero-mean
solution
\begin{equation}
  -\Acal_{\Theta(x,p)}\chi_{x,p}=B(x,p,\cdot),
  \qquad \Pi_{\Theta(x,p)}\chi_{x,p}=0.
\end{equation}
The second corrector $\psi_{x,p,X}$ is the zero-mean solution of the cell
equation whose right-hand side is the centered second-order transport/action
residual after inserting $\chi_{x,p}$.  The perturbed test function is
\begin{equation}
  \varphi^\varepsilon(t,x,z)
  =\varphi(t,x)+\varepsilon\chi_{x,p(t,x)}(z)
  +\varepsilon^2\psi_{x,p(t,x),X(t,x)}(z).
\end{equation}
All correctors are transfer-resolvent outputs supplied by
\PaperOne{Primitive spectral and resolvent theorem}{thm:primitive_spectral_resolvent}
and its suspension version
\PaperOne{Suspension Laplace contour and frequency partition}{lem:suspension_laplace_contour}.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Deterministic residual identity]
\label{lem:deterministic_residual_identity}
At a viscosity contact point, freeze the finite-response parameter at
$\Theta(x,D\varphi)$ and insert
\cref{def:corrector_hierarchy} into the deterministic prelimit
Hamilton-Jacobi operator.  Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L^\varepsilon\varphi^\varepsilon
  =
  \partial_t\varphi+\Hcal(x,D\varphi,D^2\varphi)+R^\varepsilon_\varphi,
\end{equation}
where $R^\varepsilon_\varphi$ is an anisotropic-duality residual satisfying, on
every compact jet window,
\begin{equation}
  |\langle R^\varepsilon_\varphi,\zeta\rangle|
  \le \omega_M(\varepsilon)
  \|\zeta\|_{\Bcal^\#}
  \bigl(1+\|\varphi\|_{C^3}\bigr),
  \qquad \omega_M(\varepsilon)\to0 .
\end{equation}
The identity contains no uncancelled $\varepsilon^{-1}$ term and no pointwise
claim that a zero-mean microscopic observable is small at a maximum point.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
All expansions are made after freezing the actual contact jet.  Write
\[
  p_\varepsilon=D\varphi(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon),\qquad
  X_\varepsilon=D^2\varphi(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon),\qquad
  \theta_\varepsilon=\Theta(x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon).
\]
The first corrector is evaluated in the fiber over $\theta_\varepsilon$ and
satisfies
\[
  -\Acal_{\theta_\varepsilon}\chi_{x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon}
  =B(x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon,\cdot).
\]
Consequently the scale-$\varepsilon^{-1}$ terms in the branchwise prelimit
operator cancel at the contact jet before any limiting passage is taken.  This
prevents an uncancelled
$\varepsilon^{-1}(p_\varepsilon-D\varphi(t_0,x_0))$ error.

The order-one part contains the finite-response action read-out and the work
created by the horizontal derivative of the first corrector.  The physical
gradient increment has the form
\[
  q_\varepsilon
  =D_x^{\mathrm{fr}}\chi_{x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon}
   +X_\varepsilon^T\boldsymbol\chi_{x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon},
\]
where $\boldsymbol\chi$ denotes the vector of first correctors for the slow
coordinates.
\PaperOne{Smooth deterministic response}{thm:smooth_deterministic_response},
combined with
\PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds},
identifies the invariant projection of this complete order-one observable with
\[
  \operatorname{tr}(D(x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon)X_\varepsilon)
  +H(x_\varepsilon,p_\varepsilon).
\]
Because $\Hcal(x,p,X)=-\operatorname{tr}(D(x,p)X)-H(x,p)$, this is exactly the
coefficient contribution appearing in
$\partial_t\varphi+\Hcal(x,D\varphi,D^2\varphi)$ after moving the prelimit
operator to the viscosity side.  The centered order-one part is solved by the
second cell equation defining $\psi_{x,p,X}$.

Every term not cancelled in these two steps has at least one small factor or a
controlled contact-jet displacement.  The list is finite: Taylor remainders of
the smooth test, horizontal products involving the normalized first and second
correctors, finite-response parameter variation on the compact jet window, and
moving-singularity boundary traces.  Paper 1 supplies the product, response, and
strip-tail bounds for these terms through
\PaperOne{Trace insertion into resolvent words}{lem:trace_resolvent_insertion},
\PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds},
and \PaperOne{Finite regularity-loss budget}{thm:regularity_loss_budget}.
Pairing with $\zeta\in\Bcal^\#$ therefore gives the stated residual estimate
with $\omega_M(\varepsilon)\to0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Contact-frozen perturbed tests]
\label{lem:contact_frozen_perturbed_tests}
Let $\varphi\in C^3$ touch the upper half-relaxed limit strictly at
$(t_0,x_0)$.  Then, for $\varepsilon$ small, there are prelimit contact points
$(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon,z_\varepsilon)\to(t_0,x_0,z_0)$ outside the
zero-measure singular strata such that the perturbed test in
\cref{def:corrector_hierarchy}, frozen at
$(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon)$ and normalized by subtracting its microscopic
value at that contact point, is an admissible upper viscosity-duality test for
$u^\varepsilon$.  The analogous lower-contact statement holds for lower
half-relaxed limits.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Make the macroscopic contact strict by adding a small positive bump and later
letting the bump size go to zero.  The half-relaxed definition then gives
prelimit maximizing triples in every compact cylinder.  The iterated grazing and
multiple-collision strata have zero Liouville flux measure, and admissible
density tests have summable high-strip tails, so the triples may be chosen in
homogeneous branches.  The first and second cell equations are solved after
freezing the actual contact jet
\[
  p_\varepsilon=D\varphi(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon),\qquad
  X_\varepsilon=D^2\varphi(t_\varepsilon,x_\varepsilon).
\]
Subtracting the microscopic gauge value at the contact point leaves all
generator and horizontal derivatives unchanged but makes the contact equality
valid for the normalized test.  This is the point that replaces any invalid
claim that a zero-mean corrector is pointwise small at a maximum.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Subsolution and supersolution residuals]
\label{prop:subsuper_residuals}
The upper half-relaxed limit of the deterministic prelimit solutions is a
viscosity subsolution of the effective HJB equation, and the lower half-relaxed
limit is a viscosity supersolution.  In both cases the only microscopic input
is \cref{lem:deterministic_residual_identity}; singular-billiard estimates enter
only through the named Paper 1 interface in \cref{ass:paper1_response_input}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For the subsolution inequality, let $\varphi$ touch the upper relaxed limit from
above.  Use \cref{lem:contact_frozen_perturbed_tests} to choose homogeneous
prelimit contact points and the normalized contact-frozen perturbed test
$\varphi^\varepsilon$.  Applying the prelimit viscosity-duality subsolution
inequality to this test and then using
\cref{lem:deterministic_residual_identity} gives
\[
  \partial_t\varphi+\Hcal(x,D\varphi,D^2\varphi)
  \le
  |\langle R^\varepsilon_\varphi,\zeta_\varepsilon\rangle|.
\]
The residual bound is uniform on compact jet windows and bounded admissible
density balls, hence the right-hand side tends to zero.  This gives the
subsolution inequality.  The lower-contact construction in
\cref{lem:contact_frozen_perturbed_tests} is identical, and the
viscosity-duality inequality is reversed; this gives the supersolution
inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Comparison modulus for the derived HJB]
\label{prop:comparison_modulus}
On every compact jet window, the Hamiltonian derived in
\cref{def:effective_coefficients} satisfies the Crandall-Ishii continuity
modulus required for viscosity comparison.  More precisely, if
$X,Y\in\mathrm{Sym}_m$ and $\lambda>0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
  -3\lambda
  \begin{pmatrix} I&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}
  \le
  \begin{pmatrix} X&0\\0&-Y\end{pmatrix}
  \le
  3\lambda
  \begin{pmatrix} I&-I\\-I&I\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
then there is a modulus $\omega_M$ such that
\begin{equation}
  \Hcal(y,p,Y)-\Hcal(x,p,X)
  \le
  \omega_M\!\left(|x-y|(1+|p|)+\lambda |x-y|^2\right)
\end{equation}
for all $(x,y,p,X,Y)$ in that window.  The modulus is a deterministic
consequence of the finite-response saturation, Paper 1's smooth-response and
multi-response bounds, and the Green-Kubo factorization of the diffusion tensor.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\PaperOne{Smooth deterministic response}{thm:smooth_deterministic_response}
and \PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds}
give the required horizontal regularity of the resolvent outputs that define
$D$ and $H$.  Finite-response compactness keeps the parameter selector, branch
charts, invariant projectors, and port derivatives in one compact family on the
chosen jet window.  Hence
\[
  \|D(x,p)-D(y,p)\|+|H(x,p)-H(y,p)|
  \le C_M(1+|p|)|x-y|.
\]
The Green-Kubo construction gives a correlation Hilbert factorization
$D=\Sigma\Sigma^*$ with
\[
  \|\Sigma(x,p)-\Sigma(y,p)\|_{\operatorname{HS}}^2
  \le C_M(1+|p|)|x-y|.
\]
Apply the Ishii matrix inequality to the vectors
$(\Sigma(x,p)^*\xi,\Sigma(y,p)^*\xi)$ and pass through finite-rank projections
in the correlation Hilbert bundle.  This yields
\[
  \operatorname{tr}(D(x,p)X)-\operatorname{tr}(D(y,p)Y)
  \le C_M\lambda |x-y|^2 .
\]
Combining the trace estimate with the Hamiltonian Lipschitz estimate gives the
displayed modulus for $\Hcal(y,p,Y)-\Hcal(x,p,X)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Comparison for the derived HJB]
\label{thm:comparison_derived_hjb}
Let $u$ be a bounded upper semicontinuous viscosity subsolution and let $v$ be a
bounded lower semicontinuous viscosity supersolution of
\begin{equation}
  \partial_t w+\Hcal(x,Dw,D^2w)=0
\end{equation}
on $[0,T]$.  If $u(T,\cdot)\le v(T,\cdot)$ at the terminal time, then $u\le v$.
Consequently the effective HJB in \cref{thm:main_hjb_limit} has at most one
bounded viscosity solution in the comparison class used here.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that $\sup(u-v)=\delta>0$.  After the usual compact localization in the
viscosity-comparison framework of
\cite{CrandallIshiiLions1992,FlemingSoner2006},
choose $\lambda\to\infty$, $\beta\downarrow0$, and $\eta\downarrow0$, and
maximize
\[
  u(t,x)-v(s,y)-\frac{\lambda}{2}|x-y|^2
  -\frac{|t-s|^2}{2\beta}-\eta(T-t)^{-1}.
\]
The terminal penalty and the terminal ordering force the doubled maximizer into
the parabolic interior for small parameters.  Standard doubled-variable
estimates give
\[
  \lambda |x_\lambda-y_\lambda|^2\to0,\qquad
  |t_\lambda-s_\lambda|^2/\beta\to0 .
\]
The parabolic Ishii lemma supplies jets with common spatial gradient
$p_\lambda=\lambda(x_\lambda-y_\lambda)$ and matrices $X_\lambda,Y_\lambda$
satisfying the block inequality in \cref{prop:comparison_modulus}.  Applying
the subsolution inequality to $u$, the supersolution inequality to $v$, and
subtracting gives
\[
  \frac{\eta}{(T-t_\lambda)^2}
  \le
  \omega_M\!\left(|x_\lambda-y_\lambda|(1+|p_\lambda|)
  +\lambda |x_\lambda-y_\lambda|^2\right)+o_\beta(1).
\]
The right-hand side tends to zero in the comparison limit, while the barrier
term is strictly positive.  This contradiction proves $u\le v$.
\end{proof}

\section{Deterministic HJB Limit}

\begin{theorem}[Deterministic billiards to nonconvex HJB]
\label{thm:main_hjb_limit}
Assume the primitive billiard geometry, the finite-response mechanical port, and
the companion theorem
\PaperOne{First-principles response package}{thm:main_response_package}.  Let
$u^\varepsilon$ be the prelimit viscosity-duality solution generated by the
deterministic slow-fast billiard system.  Then $u^\varepsilon$ converges locally
uniformly in the macroscopic variables, after the anisotropic microscopic
pairing and Liouville-a.e. identification, to the unique viscosity solution $u$ of
\begin{equation}
  \partial_t u+\Hcal(x,Du,D^2u)=0,
  \qquad u(T,x)=\varphi(x).
\end{equation}
Every coefficient in $\Hcal$ is a deterministic transfer-resolvent output.  No
stochastic microscopic limit theorem, independence postulate, BSDE
representation, or Girsanov formula is used in the derivation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define the upper and lower half-relaxed paired envelopes of
$u^\varepsilon$ on a fixed compact macroscopic cylinder and compact cotangent
window.  The prelimit viscosity-duality comparison estimate gives bounded
macroscopic equicontinuity, while compactness of the admissible density bundle
prevents escape of mass into grazing strips.  The terminal condition passes
directly because $u^\varepsilon(T,x,z)=\varphi(x)$ is independent of the
microscopic state.

By \cref{prop:subsuper_residuals}, the upper envelope is a viscosity
subsolution of the effective HJB and the lower envelope is a viscosity
supersolution.  The comparison theorem \cref{thm:comparison_derived_hjb} gives
upper envelope $\le$ lower envelope; the opposite inequality is part of the
definition of relaxed limits.  Hence the two envelopes coincide with the unique
viscosity solution $u$.

The residual constants in \cref{lem:deterministic_residual_identity} are uniform
over bounded admissible density balls and compact contact-jet windows, so the
paired convergence is uniform on those windows.  The Liouville-a.e. microscopic
state statement follows by applying the paired convergence to a countable
homogeneous-rectangle density basis and then using the deterministic branchwise
oscillation modulus.  The exceptional set is the union of the iterated singular
orbit set with countably many density-basis null sets, and therefore has
Liouville measure zero.  No stochastic microscopic limit theorem enters the
argument.
\end{proof}

\section{Nonconvexity and theta-Expectations}

\begin{theorem}[Nonconvex theta-expectation]
\label{thm:nonconvex_theta_expectation}
There are finite-response billiard ports for which $p\mapsto H(x,p)$ is locally
nonconvex.  For such ports, the nonlinear semigroup generated by
\cref{thm:main_hjb_limit} is not generally subadditive:
\begin{equation}
  \Etheta_t[\varphi+\psi]\ne
  \Etheta_t[\varphi]+\Etheta_t[\psi]
\end{equation}
in general, and the subadditive inequality may fail in either direction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the concrete port in \cref{prop:inspectable_nonconvexity_coefficient} and
choose $x$ in the open set where
\(\mathfrak c_e(x)=\frac{d^2}{ds^2}H(x,se)|_{s=0}<0\).  For small \(a>0\),
\[
  H(x,2ae)-2H(x,ae)=\mathfrak c_e(x)a^2+o(a^2)<0 .
\]
Choose smooth terminal payoffs $\varphi,\psi$ supported in a coordinate chart so
that at $x$
\[
  D\varphi=D\psi=ae,\qquad D^2\varphi=D^2\psi=0.
\]
For the terminal-value convention in \cref{def:theta_expectation_semigroup}, the
short-time viscosity expansion at such a smooth contact is
\[
  \Etheta_t[\varphi](x)=\varphi(x)-tH(x,ae)+o(t),
  \qquad
  \Etheta_t[\varphi+\psi](x)=\varphi(x)+\psi(x)-tH(x,2ae)+o(t).
\]
Therefore
\[
  \Etheta_t[\varphi+\psi](x)-\Etheta_t[\varphi](x)-\Etheta_t[\psi](x)
  =
  -t\{H(x,2ae)-2H(x,ae)\}+o(t)>0
\]
for small $t>0$.  This violates subadditivity.  Changing the sign of the
microscopic response direction gives the opposite Hamiltonian defect when that
direction is desired, so the failure is not tied to a convex/sublinear
special case.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[theta-expectation semigroup]
\label{def:theta_expectation_semigroup}
For a terminal payoff $\varphi$, define
\begin{equation}
  \Etheta_t[\varphi](x)=u(0,x),
\end{equation}
where $u$ is the viscosity solution of the HJB equation in
\cref{thm:main_hjb_limit} on the interval $[0,t]$ with terminal payoff
$\varphi$ at time $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Basic theta-expectation properties]
\label{thm:theta_expectation_properties}
The semigroup $\Etheta_t$ is constant preserving, monotone, and dynamically
consistent.  It is generally nonlinear and, by
\cref{thm:nonconvex_theta_expectation}, it is not a subadditive
\(G\)-expectation in the sense of \cite{Peng2019} in general.
\end{theorem}

\section{Concrete Example Requirement}

\begin{definition}[Concrete finite-horizon triangular Lorentz cell]
\label{def:triangular_lorentz_cell}
Let $\Lambda$ be the triangular lattice generated by
\[
  a_1=(1,0),\qquad a_2=(1/2,\sqrt3/2),
\]
and let $\T_\Lambda^2=\R^2/\Lambda$.  Fix a circular scatterer centered at the
lattice point with radius
\[
  r_0\in\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3},\,\frac12\right).
\]
The billiard cell is $\T_\Lambda^2\setminus B(0,r_0)$.  This is the standard
finite-horizon triangular Lorentz cell: the lower bound on $r_0$ blocks the
maximal triangular-lattice corridors, while the upper bound keeps neighboring
scatterers disjoint.  Small $C^{r+3}$ normal deformations of the boundary stay
inside the same finite-horizon dispersing class.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Two-mode finite-response port on the concrete cell]
\label{def:two_mode_port_example}
Start from \cref{def:triangular_lorentz_cell}.  Write the circular boundary in
arclength $s\in\R/(2\pi r_0\mathbb Z)$ and set
\[
  \beta(t)=
  \begin{cases}
  \exp\!\bigl(-1/(1-t^2)\bigr),& |t|<1,\\
  0,& |t|\ge1.
  \end{cases}
\]
Choose $\delta<\pi r_0/12$ and define the normalized arclength bumps
\[
  \beta_{s_0,\delta}(s)
  =
  \frac{\beta(\dist(s,s_0)/\delta)}
  {\|\beta(\dist(\cdot,s_0)/\delta)\|_{C^{r+3}}}.
\]
Set
\[
  \psi_1=\beta_{0,\delta},
  \qquad
  \psi_2=\beta_{2\pi r_0/3,\delta}.
\]
These are disjoint nonnegative $C^{r+3}$ normal deformation modes with
$C^{r+3}$ norm one.  The deformed boundary is
\[
  q(s,\theta)=q(s,0)+\theta_1\psi_1(s)n(s)
  +\theta_2\psi_2(s)n(s),
  \qquad \theta\in[-\theta_*,\theta_*]^2 .
\]
For $\theta_*$ sufficiently small, the deformed cell remains strictly
dispersing and finite horizon by openness of the curvature, separation, and
corridor-blocking inequalities.
For a fixed macroscopic direction $e\in\R^m$, define a microscopic
finite-response selector
\begin{equation}
  \Theta(x,p)=
  \theta_0+\alpha_1(x)(p\cdot e)e_1
  +\alpha_2(x)(p\cdot e)^2 e_2 ,
\end{equation}
where $e_1,e_2$ are the coordinate directions in parameter space.  The centered
drift read-out and action read-out have branchwise smooth expansions
\begin{align}
  B(x,p,z)&=B_0(x,z)+(p\cdot e)B_1(x,z)+(p\cdot e)^2B_2(x,z)+O(|p|^3),\\
  V(x,p,z)&=V_0(x,z)-\lambda(x)\eta(z)(p\cdot e)^2
  +\kappa(x)\eta(z)(p\cdot e)^4+O(|p|^5),
\end{align}
with $\lambda(x)>0$, $\kappa(x)>0$, and a nonnegative branchwise smooth
observable $\eta$ with positive billiard average.  These read-outs are part of
the primitive finite-response port; they are fixed before the effective
Hamiltonian is computed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Concrete observable and dominance constant]
\label{def:concrete_eta_dominance}
Let
\[
  \chi_\eta(s)=\beta_{4\pi r_0/3,\delta}(s).
\]
This bump is supported on a boundary arc disjoint from the supports of
$\psi_1,\psi_2$.  Define
\begin{equation}
  \eta(s,\varphi)=\chi_\eta(s)\cos^2\varphi .
\end{equation}
Then $\langle\eta\rangle_{\theta_0}>0$.  Let $C_{\rm resp}(x)$ be the
Paper-1-exported response bound defined in \cref{def:Cresp_bound}.  It controls
all second-order invariant-density and corrector-resolvent terms appearing in
\cref{prop:inspectable_nonconvexity_coefficient}, excluding the direct action
average.  The dominance condition is
\begin{equation}
  2\lambda(x)\langle\eta\rangle_{\theta_0}
  >
  C_{\rm resp}(x)+\delta_x
  \qquad(\delta_x>0).
\end{equation}
Under this checkable inequality the directional Taylor coefficient is strictly
negative.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Paper 1 response bound used by the concrete example]
\label{def:Cresp_bound}
For the concrete port, let the norms of the primitive read-outs be measured in
the response domain exported by Paper 1 with the eight-derivative loss recorded
in \PaperOne{Finite regularity-loss budget}{thm:regularity_loss_budget}.
Denote by
\[
  \mathfrak C_{\Pi,2},\qquad
  \mathfrak C_{\mathcal R,2},\qquad
  \mathfrak C_{\mathrm{tr},2},\qquad
  \mathfrak C_{\mathrm{loss}}
\]
the uniform constants exported by the following Paper 1 components.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.70\linewidth}}
\hline
Constant & Paper 1 source \\
\hline
$\mathfrak C_{\Pi,2}$ &
\PaperOne{Smooth deterministic response}{thm:smooth_deterministic_response}
and \PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds}. \\
$\mathfrak C_{\mathcal R,2}$ &
\PaperOne{Primitive spectral and resolvent theorem}{thm:primitive_spectral_resolvent},
\PaperOne{Suspension Laplace contour and frequency partition}{lem:suspension_laplace_contour},
and \PaperOne{Uniform multi-response bounds}{prop:uniform_multiresponse_bounds}. \\
$\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{tr},2}$ &
\PaperOne{Trace insertion into resolvent words}{lem:trace_resolvent_insertion}
together with the moving-boundary trace estimates. \\
$\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{loss}}$ &
\PaperOne{Finite regularity-loss budget}{thm:regularity_loss_budget}. \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
They control, respectively, second derivatives of invariant projectors, second
derivatives of reduced observable resolvents, moving-trace insertions in
differentiated resolvent words, and the finite regularity-loss embedding.
Define
\begin{align}
  C_{\rm resp}(x)
  &:=
  \mathfrak C_{\mathrm{loss}}
  \Big[
    \mathfrak C_{\Pi,2}\|V_0(x,\cdot)\|_{r+8}
    +\mathfrak C_{\mathcal R,2}
      \bigl(\|B_1(x,\cdot)\|_{r+8}^2+\|B_2(x,\cdot)\|_{r+8}\bigr)
      \notag\\
  &\hspace{3.0cm}
    +\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{tr},2}
      \bigl(\|\psi_1\|_{C^{r+8}}+\|\psi_2\|_{C^{r+8}}\bigr)
      \bigl(\|V_0(x,\cdot)\|_{r+8}+\|B_1(x,\cdot)\|_{r+8}\bigr)
  \Big].
\end{align}
All constants in this display are downstream of
\PaperOne{First-principles response package}{thm:main_response_package} and are
produced before the HJB theorem.  No effective Hamiltonian coefficient is
included as input.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Response-bound provenance for the dominance test]
\label{prop:Cresp_controls_response_terms}
For the concrete port in \cref{def:two_mode_port_example}, the sum of all
second-order invariant-density response terms and corrector/resolvent response
terms in the directional coefficient $\mathfrak c_e(x)$ is bounded in absolute
value by $C_{\rm resp}(x)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The second derivative of the invariant average is controlled by the projector
derivative constant $\mathfrak C_{\Pi,2}$.  The derivatives of the first
corrector and of the second-order corrector are controlled by the differentiated
reduced-resolvent words, hence by $\mathfrak C_{\mathcal R,2}$.  Terms in which
the differentiated homogeneous partition or moving singularity boundary enters
a resolvent word are controlled by
\PaperOne{Trace insertion into resolvent words}{lem:trace_resolvent_insertion},
represented here by $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{tr},2}$.  The downstream coefficient
calculation consumes the derivative loss in
\PaperOne{Finite regularity-loss budget}{thm:regularity_loss_budget},
represented here by $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{loss}}$.  Multiplying these constants
by the displayed primitive read-out norms gives exactly the bound in
\cref{def:Cresp_bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Inspectable nonconvexity coefficient]
\label{prop:inspectable_nonconvexity_coefficient}
For the example target in \cref{def:two_mode_port_example}, define the
deterministic Taylor coefficient
\begin{equation}
  \mathfrak c_e(x)=
  \left.\frac{d^2}{ds^2}H(x,se)\right|_{s=0},
\end{equation}
where $H$ is computed from the transfer-resolvent formula in
\cref{def:effective_coefficients}.  The coefficient $\mathfrak c_e(x)$ is an
explicit finite sum of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},wide,labelindent=0pt]
  \item direct action averages from $\partial_s^2V(x,se,\cdot)|_{s=0}$;
  \item response derivatives of the invariant density under
  $\Theta(x,se)$;
  \item corrector/resolvent pairings involving
  $\partial_sB(x,se,\cdot)|_{s=0}$ and
  $\partial_s^2B(x,se,\cdot)|_{s=0}$.
\end{enumerate}
If the direct negative action term dominates the two response-corrector terms,
so that $\mathfrak c_e(x)<0$ on some open macroscopic set, then
$p\mapsto H(x,p)$ is locally nonconvex there.  Consequently
\cref{thm:nonconvex_theta_expectation} applies to concrete payoffs whose
contact gradients lie in that set.  For the concrete choice in
\cref{def:concrete_eta_dominance}, the sufficient dominance condition is
\[
  2\lambda(x)\langle\eta\rangle_{\theta_0}
  >C_{\rm resp}(x)+\delta_x .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Differentiate the deterministic coefficient formula in
\cref{def:effective_coefficients} twice along $p=se$.
\PaperOne{Smooth deterministic response}{thm:smooth_deterministic_response} and
\PaperOne{Moving-singularity response theorem}{thm:moving_singularity_response}
justify differentiating the invariant density, projectors, and reduced
resolvent in the moving billiard fiber, while
\PaperOne{Trace insertion into resolvent words}{lem:trace_resolvent_insertion}
controls trace terms inside differentiated resolvent words.  Thus the second
derivative splits into the direct action term, the invariant-density response
term, and the corrector/resolvent response term listed in the statement.

For the concrete read-out in \cref{def:two_mode_port_example}, the direct action
contribution is
\[
  \left.\frac{d^2}{ds^2}
  \langle-\lambda(x)\eta\,s^2\rangle_{\theta_0}\right|_{s=0}
  =
  -2\lambda(x)\langle\eta\rangle_{\theta_0}.
\]
By \cref{prop:Cresp_controls_response_terms}, the absolute value of all
remaining second-order response-corrector contributions is bounded by
$C_{\rm resp}(x)$.
The dominance condition in \cref{def:concrete_eta_dominance} therefore gives
\[
  \mathfrak c_e(x)\le -\delta_x<0 .
\]
Taylor's formula then gives
\[
  H(x,se)+H(x,-se)-2H(x,0)
  =\mathfrak c_e(x)s^2+o(s^2)<0
\]
for all sufficiently small nonzero $s$.  Hence $p\mapsto H(x,p)$ is locally
nonconvex, and the same negative two-point defect is the short-time
non-subadditivity input used in \cref{thm:nonconvex_theta_expectation}.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Citation-provenance status.}
The example is now inspectable at the level needed by Paper 2: the bump
functions $\psi_1,\psi_2,\chi_\eta$ are explicit, the finite-horizon base table
and dominance inequality are fixed in
\cref{def:triangular_lorentz_cell,def:concrete_eta_dominance}, and the analytic
constant $C_{\rm resp}(x)$ is tied to the named Paper 1 response theorems in
\cref{def:Cresp_bound}.  The bibliography in this paper anchors only the
macroscopic viscosity, homogenization, and nonlinear-expectation tools listed
above.  The singular-billiard literature is attached to the Paper 1 theorem
statements rather than repeated here.

\section{Use by the Representation Paper}

The representation-calculus paper may take $\Etheta_t$ and its generator as
inputs.  BSDE, Girsanov, and Cameron-Martin formulae should remain downstream
representations and should not be used to prove \cref{thm:main_hjb_limit}.

\title[Representation Calculus for theta-Expectations]{Representation Calculus for theta-Expectations}
\author{Qian Qi}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
This paper develops the representation theory that lies downstream of the
first-principles theta-expectation construction.  The nonlinear semigroup and
its nonconvex HJB generator are taken as outputs of the companion
homogenization paper.  After this input is fixed, each sufficiently regular
payoff determines a linearized parabolic generator, a carre-du-champ, a
calibrated diffusion representation, a decoupled BSDE, and a semigroup-level
Cameron-Martin--Girsanov formula.  These objects represent the already-derived
semigroup; they are not inputs to the deterministic billiard derivation.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

This is the third article in the sequence.  Paper 1 proves the singular
billiard response package.  Paper 2 uses that package to derive the nonconvex
HJB equation and the theta-expectation semigroup from deterministic billiards.
The present paper begins only after those two steps are complete.

\paragraph{Representation, not derivation.}
The central point is the payoff dependence of every classical probabilistic
representation.  A genuinely nonlinear HJB semigroup cannot be represented by a
single classical martingale problem for all test functions.  Once a terminal
payoff is fixed, however, its decoupling field freezes the nonlinear generator
into an ordinary linear parabolic operator.  Diffusions, BSDEs, and Girsanov
formulae are then available for that calibrated linear problem.

\subsection{Provenance and dependency guardrail}

The stochastic-analysis tools used below are classical: the martingale-problem
representation follows \cite{stroock2007multidimensional}, the parabolic and
viscosity stability language follows
\cite{CrandallIshiiLions1992,FlemingSoner2006}, the BSDE convention follows
\cite{PardouxPeng1992}, and the stochastic-calculus/Girsanov notation follows
\cite{protter2012stochastic}.  Nonlinear expectation terminology follows
\cite{Peng2019}.  These references are used only after the deterministic
theta-expectation semigroup has been derived in the companion HJB paper.

\section{Input from the theta-Expectation Paper}

\begin{assumption}[Derived nonlinear semigroup]
\label{ass:theta_semigroup_input}
The companion theta-expectation paper has constructed coefficients
\[
  D(x,p)\in\R^{d\times d}_{\mathrm{sym},+},
  \qquad H(x,p)\in\R,
\]
from deterministic billiard response theory and finite-response mechanics.  It
has also proved comparison and uniqueness for the terminal-value HJB equation
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:input_hjb}
  -\partial_t u-\Tr(D(x,\nabla u)\nabla^2u)-H(x,\nabla u)=0,
  \qquad u(T,\cdot)=\phi .
\end{equation}
The normalized semigroup is
\begin{equation}
  \Etheta_{t,T}[\phi](x)=u(t,x).
\end{equation}
It is constant preserving, cash additive, monotone, and time consistent, and it
is generally nonlinear and not subadditive.
\end{assumption}

\begin{remark}
\Cref{ass:theta_semigroup_input} is the only connection to deterministic
billiards used in this paper.  All microscopic response estimates and the HJB
homogenization theorem belong to the companion papers.
\end{remark}

\begin{assumption}[Representation window]
\label{ass:representation_window}
Fix a compact cylinder \(Q=[t_0,T]\times K\) and a compact jet set containing
all gradients and Hessians used below.  On \(Q\), the payoff under discussion
has a decoupling field \(u\) that is either \(C^{1,2}\) or the locally uniform
limit of smooth uniformly parabolic regularizations.  The coefficients
\(D,H\) and their first \(p\)-derivatives are bounded and continuous on this
jet set.  In the nondegenerate diffusion and BSDE statements, also assume
\(a^u=2D(x,\nabla u)\) is uniformly positive definite and has a chosen square
root \(\sigma^u\) with the regularity needed for the corresponding stochastic
equations.
\end{assumption}

\section{Linearity Obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Linearity obstruction]
\label{thm:linearity_obstruction}
Let $\Gcal$ be an operator on a vector space of smooth tests.  If there is a
single probability law under which
\begin{equation}
  f(t,X_t)-f(0,X_0)-\int_0^t \Gcal f(s,X_s)\,ds
\end{equation}
is a martingale for every test $f$, then $\Gcal$ is additive on that class.
Consequently a genuinely nonlinear operator
\begin{equation}
  \Gcal f=\partial_t f+\Tr(D(x,\nabla f)\nabla^2f)+H(x,\nabla f)
\end{equation}
cannot be the generator of one classical martingale problem for all tests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the martingale property to $f$, $g$, and $f+g$.  Subtracting the three
martingales gives a finite-variation martingale with drift
\[
  \Gcal(f+g)-\Gcal f-\Gcal g .
\]
It is constant, so the drift vanishes along the support of the law.  Varying
the initial point gives additivity on the test class.  Nonlinear dependence on
$\nabla f$ or $\nabla^2 f$ violates this except in accidentally linear cases.
\end{proof}

\section{Payoff-Dependent Linearization}

\begin{definition}[Calibrated linear generator]
\label{def:calibrated_linear_generator}
Work on a representation window satisfying
\cref{ass:representation_window}.  For a fixed terminal payoff \(\phi\), let
\(u\) be its decoupling field.  Set
\begin{align}
  a^u(t,x)&=2D(x,\nabla u(t,x)),\\
  b^u_k(t,x)&=\partial_{p_k}H(x,\nabla u(t,x))
  +\sum_{i,j}\partial_{p_k}D_{ij}(x,\nabla u(t,x))\,\partial_{ij}u(t,x).
\end{align}
The payoff-calibrated generator is
\begin{equation}
  \Lcal_t^u f(x)=\frac12\Tr(a^u(t,x)\nabla^2 f(x))
  +b^u(t,x)\cdot\nabla f(x).
\end{equation}
Its carre-du-champ is
\begin{equation}
  \Gamma_t^u(f,g)
  =\frac12\bigl(\Lcal_t^u(fg)-f\Lcal_t^ug-g\Lcal_t^uf\bigr)
  =\frac12\nabla f^\top a^u\nabla g.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Linearized representation for a fixed payoff]
\label{thm:linearized_representation}
Let $u$ be the smooth solution of \eqref{eq:input_hjb} with terminal payoff
$\phi$.  If $u^\delta$ solves the same HJB equation with terminal payoff
$\phi+\delta\eta$ and $u^\delta=u+\delta v+o(\delta)$ locally uniformly, then
$v$ solves
\begin{equation}
  -\partial_t v-\Lcal_t^u v=0,\qquad v(T,\cdot)=\eta .
\end{equation}
Thus the first variation of the nonlinear semigroup at $\phi$ is represented
by the linear parabolic equation generated by $\Lcal^u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Insert $u^\delta=u+\delta v+o(\delta)$ into the HJB operator and differentiate
at $\delta=0$.  The derivative of the Hessian term gives
$\Tr(D(x,\nabla u)\nabla^2 v)$ plus the drift correction
\[
  \sum_{i,j,k}\partial_{p_k}D_{ij}(x,\nabla u)\,\partial_{ij}u\,\partial_k v.
\]
The derivative of $H$ gives $\partial_pH(x,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla v$.  These
terms are exactly $\Lcal_t^u v$ with the sign convention above.
\end{proof}

\section{Calibrated Diffusion Representation}

\begin{theorem}[Smooth nondegenerate calibrated diffusion]
\label{thm:smooth_diffusion_representation}
Assume $a^u$ is uniformly positive definite and the coefficients in
\cref{def:calibrated_linear_generator} are regular enough for the martingale
problem of $\Lcal^u$ to be well posed.  Then the derivative semigroup in
\cref{thm:linearized_representation} has the classical diffusion
representation
\begin{equation}
  dX_s=b^u(s,X_s)\,ds+\sigma^u(s,X_s)\,dW_s,
  \qquad \sigma^u(\sigma^u)^\top=a^u .
\end{equation}
The representing law depends on the payoff through $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For fixed $u$, the operator $\Lcal^u$ is linear.  The standard parabolic
martingale-problem representation
\cite{stroock2007multidimensional,FlemingSoner2006} applies to that linear
operator.  The
dependence on $\phi$ enters through the coefficients $a^u$ and $b^u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Degenerate representation by viscosity regularization]
\label{thm:regularized_diffusion_representation}
Suppose the viscosity solution $u$ is the locally uniform limit of smooth
solutions $u^\varepsilon$ to uniformly parabolic regularizations with
$D$ replaced by $D+\varepsilon I$.  The corresponding calibrated linear
diffusion semigroups converge locally uniformly to the payoff-calibrated
representation of the original degenerate HJB semigroup.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each $\varepsilon>0$, the matrix $2(D+\varepsilon I)$ is uniformly positive
and gives a classical diffusion representation.  Stability of viscosity
solutions \cite{CrandallIshiiLions1992,FlemingSoner2006} and stability of the
linearized coefficients along the smooth regularization identify the locally
uniform limit with the derivative of the original nonlinear semigroup.  The
construction starts after the effective HJB has been derived.
\end{proof}

\section{BSDE Representation}

\begin{lemma}[Gradient variable versus BSDE integrand]
\label{lem:gradient_z_conversion}
In the representation window, the HJB gradient variable is
\[
  p(t,x)=\nabla u(t,x).
\]
The BSDE martingale integrand is not \(p\).  It is
\[
  Z_t=\sigma(X_t,p(t,X_t))^\top p(t,X_t).
\]
When \(\sigma^\top\) is invertible on the chosen nondegenerate jet region, one
may recover \(p=(\sigma^\top)^{-1}Z\).  All BSDE drivers below use this
conversion only after the payoff and decoupling field are fixed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Decoupled FBSDE for a smooth payoff]
\label{thm:fbsde_representation}
Let $u$ be a smooth HJB solution and assume
\[
  \sigma(x,p)\sigma(x,p)^\top=2D(x,p)
\]
is nondegenerate on the relevant jet range.  Let $X$ solve
\begin{equation}
  dX_t=b^u(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t,\nabla u(t,X_t))\,dW_t .
\end{equation}
Set
\[
  Y_t=u(t,X_t),\qquad
  Z_t=\sigma(X_t,\nabla u(t,X_t))^\top\nabla u(t,X_t).
\]
Then $(X,Y,Z)$ satisfies the decoupled BSDE
\begin{equation}
  dY_t=-g(t,X_t,Z_t)\,dt+Z_t\,dW_t,
  \qquad Y_T=\phi(X_T),
\end{equation}
where, writing $p=(\sigma^\top)^{-1}Z$,
\begin{equation}
  g(t,x,Z)=H(x,p)-b^u(t,x)\cdot p .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Ito's formula to $Y_t=u(t,X_t)$, using the convention in
\cref{lem:gradient_z_conversion}.  The martingale coefficient is
$Z_t=\sigma^\top\nabla u$.  The drift is
\[
  \partial_tu+b^u\cdot\nabla u+\frac12\Tr(\sigma\sigma^\top\nabla^2u)
  =\partial_tu+b^u\cdot p+\Tr(D\nabla^2u).
\]
Using the HJB equation, this equals $b^u\cdot p-H(x,p)=-g(t,x,Z)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Sign Convention and Parabolic Orientation}

\begin{proposition}[Parabolic orientation ledger]
\label{prop:parabolic_orientation_ledger}
The terminal-value convention in \cref{eq:input_hjb}, the calibrated diffusion
orientation, and the BSDE sign convention are consistent as follows.  For
\[
  Y_s=u(s,X_s),\qquad
  Z_s=\sigma(X_s,\nabla u(s,X_s))^\top\nabla u(s,X_s),
\]
the differential form
\[
  dY_s=-g(s,X_s,Z_s)\,ds+Z_s\,dW_s
\]
is equivalent to the backward integral equation
\[
  Y_t=\phi(X_T)+\int_t^T g(s,X_s,Z_s)\,ds
       -\int_t^T Z_s\,dW_s.
\]
If one writes forward parabolic time as \(\tau=T-t\) and
\(U(\tau,x)=u(T-\tau,x)\), then the same terminal-value HJB becomes
\[
  \partial_\tau U
  -\Tr\bigl(D(x,\nabla U)\nabla^2U\bigr)-H(x,\nabla U)=0,
  \qquad U(0,\cdot)=\phi .
\]
Thus no sign is changed when passing from the terminal HJB to the backward
BSDE; only the time orientation changes.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For the calibrated diffusion, Ito's formula gives
\[
  dY_s
  =
  \bigl(\partial_su+b^u\cdot\nabla u
  +\Tr(D(x,\nabla u)\nabla^2u)\bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds
  +Z_s\,dW_s .
\]
The terminal-value HJB gives
\[
  \partial_su+\Tr(D(x,\nabla u)\nabla^2u)=-H(x,\nabla u),
\]
so the drift is \(b^u\cdot p-H(x,p)=-g(s,x,Z)\).  Integrating the differential
identity from \(t\) to \(T\) gives the displayed BSDE.  The forward-time
equation follows by the substitution \(U(\tau,x)=u(T-\tau,x)\), for which
\(\partial_\tau U=-\partial_tu\).
\end{proof}

\section{Nonlinear Cameron-Martin--Girsanov Formula}

\begin{definition}[Hamiltonian shift]
\label{def:hamiltonian_shift}
For a deterministic shift $h(t,x)$ define
\begin{align}
  H^h(x,p)&=H(x,p+h)-H(x,h),\\
  D^h(x,p)&=D(x,p+h).
\end{align}
The shifted semigroup is generated by the HJB equation with $D,H$ replaced by
$D^h,H^h$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Semigroup-level Cameron-Martin formula]
\label{thm:nonlinear_cm_formula}
Let $u_h$ solve the shifted equation.  Then $u_h$ also solves the unshifted
equation with deterministic generator defect
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lambda_h}
  \Lambda_h(t,x,p,X)
  =\Tr\bigl((D(x,p+h)-D(x,p))X\bigr)
  +H(x,p+h)-H(x,h)-H(x,p).
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
  -\partial_tu_h-\Tr(D(x,\nabla u_h)\nabla^2u_h)-H(x,\nabla u_h)
  -\Lambda_h(t,x,\nabla u_h,\nabla^2u_h)=0.
\end{equation}
When $D$ is independent of $p$ and $H$ is linear-quadratic, this identity
reduces after linearization to the classical Cameron-Martin--Girsanov drift
tilt \cite{protter2012stochastic}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Insert the definitions of $D^h$ and $H^h$ into the shifted HJB equation.  Add
and subtract the unshifted terms
\[
  \Tr(D(x,\nabla u_h)\nabla^2u_h)+H(x,\nabla u_h).
\]
The remainder is exactly \eqref{eq:lambda_h}.  The linear-quadratic special
case gives
$H(x,p+h)-H(x,h)-H(x,p)=p^\top a(x)h$, the usual drift-tilt term for the
payoff-calibrated linear diffusion.
\end{proof}

\section{A Short Robust-Pricing Illustration}

\begin{definition}[Calibrated stress family]
\label{def:calibrated_stress_family}
Fix a terminal payoff \(\phi\) in a representation window and let
\(\mathfrak H\) be a compact family of deterministic shifts \(h(t,x)\) for
which the shifted equations in \cref{def:hamiltonian_shift} remain in the same
regularity window.  For each \(h\in\mathfrak H\), let \(u^h\) be the shifted
solution with terminal value \(\phi\).  The calibrated stress envelope is
\[
  \Pi_{\mathfrak H}\phi(t,x)
  =
  \sup_{h\in\mathfrak H} u^h(t,x).
\]
This envelope is a post-derivation stress test for the already constructed
theta-expectation semigroup, not a new primitive market model.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Robust-pricing stress test]
\label{prop:robust_pricing_stress_test}
In the smooth nondegenerate representation window, each \(h\in\mathfrak H\)
has a payoff-calibrated diffusion and BSDE representation obtained from the
shifted coefficients \(D^h,H^h\).  The envelope
\(\Pi_{\mathfrak H}\phi\) therefore records a family of calibrated drift and
Hamiltonian stresses for the fixed payoff.  When \(D\) is independent of \(p\)
and \(H\) is linear-quadratic, this reduces to the familiar drift-uncertainty
stress test after the Cameron-Martin--Girsanov tilt.  In the nonconvex
theta-expectation case the envelope should not be read as a sublinear
expectation unless the additional sublinearity inequalities are separately
verified.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For each fixed \(h\), \cref{thm:nonlinear_cm_formula} rewrites the shifted
equation as the unshifted equation plus the deterministic defect
\(\Lambda_h\).  Once the payoff and shifted decoupling field \(u^h\) are
fixed, the construction of
\cref{def:calibrated_linear_generator,thm:smooth_diffusion_representation,thm:fbsde_representation}
applies with \(D,H,u\) replaced by \(D^h,H^h,u^h\).  Compactness of
\(\mathfrak H\) and the representation-window bounds keep the family in one
local regularity class.  In the linear-quadratic case the defect is the
classical drift tilt \(p^\top a h\).  For a nonconvex Hamiltonian, taking a
supremum over calibrated stresses gives a useful pricing diagnostic, but it
does not restore the global subadditivity that Paper 2 proves can fail.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Post-derivation calibration]
\label{prop:post_derivation_calibration}
The calibrated laws and BSDEs in
\cref{thm:smooth_diffusion_representation,thm:regularized_diffusion_representation,thm:fbsde_representation}
are downstream representations of a fixed payoff.  They do not form a single
payoff-independent martingale problem and cannot be used to prove
\cref{ass:theta_semigroup_input}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The law in \cref{thm:smooth_diffusion_representation} depends on \(u\), and
\(u\) is determined by the terminal payoff through the nonlinear HJB semigroup.
Changing the payoff changes \(u\), hence changes \(a^u\), \(b^u\), the
calibrated diffusion, and the BSDE driver.  A payoff-independent law would
contradict \cref{thm:linearity_obstruction} except in accidentally linear
cases.  Therefore the logical order is acyclic: Paper 2 first supplies the
semigroup, then the present paper represents its fixed-payoff derivatives.
\end{proof}

\section{Main Representation Package}

\begin{theorem}[Representation calculus package]
\label{thm:representation_package}
Under \cref{ass:theta_semigroup_input}, every sufficiently regular terminal
payoff determines:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},wide,labelindent=0pt]
  \item a payoff-calibrated linearized generator $\Lcal^u$;
  \item a carre-du-champ $\Gamma^u$;
  \item a smooth or regularized calibrated diffusion representation;
  \item a decoupled BSDE representation on nondegenerate jet regions;
  \item a semigroup-level Cameron-Martin--Girsanov formula.
  \item a terminal-value sign-convention ledger;
  \item for any compact deterministic stress family, a calibrated
  robust-pricing stress envelope.
\end{enumerate}
All objects above are post-derivation representations of the theta-expectation
semigroup.  None is used to prove the deterministic billiard response theorem
or the HJB homogenization theorem.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Items (i) and (ii) are \cref{def:calibrated_linear_generator}.  Item (iii) is
\cref{thm:smooth_diffusion_representation,thm:regularized_diffusion_representation}.
Item (iv) is \cref{thm:fbsde_representation}.  Item (v) is
\cref{thm:nonlinear_cm_formula}.  Item (vi) is
\cref{prop:parabolic_orientation_ledger}.  Item (vii) is
\cref{def:calibrated_stress_family,prop:robust_pricing_stress_test}.  The
downstream character follows from the single input assumption
\cref{ass:theta_semigroup_input} and the calibration guardrail in
\cref{prop:post_derivation_calibration}.
\end{proof}

\section{Submission Scope}

The paper's submission version should keep smoothness, nondegeneracy, and
localization assumptions close to each representation theorem.  It should not
import billiard technical lemmas except through Paper 2's HJB theorem.  The
robust-pricing example above should remain a short illustration of calibrated
stress testing, not an additional primitive derivation.

## Response-theory referee repair — 2026-07-10

- Work root: `/home/qian-qi/paper_factory/submission/AoM/A_Theory_of__Expectations/papers/response-theory`.
- After a detailed referee critique, the manuscript was reduced to a defensible first-order observable-side response theorem. The active `main.tex` is 1,527 lines; seven inactive `\\iffalse` high-order legacy blocks and obsolete theorem-label aliases were removed. `proof-ledger-appendix.tex` remains only as a legacy audit artifact and is excluded from the build.
- The erroneous Dolgopyat claim that the full union of resonant/bad windows has length `O(|b|^{-1})` was removed; the manuscript now acknowledges the union is generally only `O(1)` and imports the BDL flow generator-resolvent estimate under an explicit uniform compatibility hypothesis rather than presenting a one-step weighted collision-operator proof.
- Fixed homogeneity-strip width `k^{-3}` plus the ordinary growth lemma is no longer used to infer arbitrary weighted moments. The single weighted moment needed for the first trace is now an explicit analytic assumption; arbitrary-order trace summability is not claimed.
- The density-side strong-recovery assertion `R^{map}B:D -> D` was removed because weak trace sources and finite prefixes were not shown to lie in the strong density space. The response formula is now posed on the observable side as `I'(0)=<rho_0,f'_0>+<L'_0 rho_0,(I-U_0)^{-1}Pi_0^perp f_0>`, with adjoint-resolvent trace regularity made explicit.
- Higher multiple-delta traces, cross-space Kato resolvent words, arbitrary resolvent-word closure, and the old `r-8` / high-order hierarchy were withdrawn from the theorem. The manuscript now uses Demers-Zhang billiard-specific anisotropic spaces/references rather than claiming that a schematic norm reconstructs their theory and BDL.
- A standalone first-transfer-derivative proposition now separates branch/interior, Jacobian, and physical-trace contributions. The rigid-scatterer-translation test now derives impact time by `tau_dot=(n dot w)/(n dot v)` and then obtains the collision-section singular-curve velocity, avoiding an invalid direct product between a physical velocity and a section-coordinate normal.
- Six consistency checks are included or explicitly required: constant observable response, mass derivative, tangential boundary reparametrization, transport-choice independence, cancellation of artificial strip-boundary center traces, and a concrete constant-speed scatterer translation.
- Remaining central mathematical risks are stated honestly in `risk-register.md` and `theorem-inventory.md`: prove the first-order weighted strip moment for the chosen space/family; prove adjoint observable-resolvent trace regularity and the needed limit interchange; verify uniform spectral constants and the exact BDL compatibility hypotheses. =
\left\{
\sum F_nz^n:
\sum e^{\delta n}\|F_n\|<\infty
\right\},
\]

以及由统一 annulus invertibility、simple isolated eigenvalue、共同 block norms 和 Cauchy estimates推出 \(H\in\mathcal W_\delta\)，而不是把它放进 RW1。

# CM2 v44 fresh top-journal referee audit — 2026-07-14 03:22 CST

- Conducted a new read-only referee audit of frozen CM2 v44 from scratch, without web access or any external Oracle and without treating the prior CLEAN audits as evidence. Frozen hashes remained unchanged: TEX `90d6aeb32bbbfaee4a1594a702ebdc842fa669591af4ef658306e3bda8b26652`; PDF `2fac4f5f6646ce8a10efb355daa0bc4580817b725d865dddf8b374a61d18075f`.
- Referee recommendation: `Reject in present form; invite resubmission after a focused reconstruction.` The fresh audit found no v43-style Fatal, but found two new formal/type-closure Major gaps at the master-`q`/actual-handler interface. Even after those are repaired, the top-journal publication-level obstacle remains that the paper proves only a strongly conditional criterion and does not jointly verify its hardest primitive interfaces on any nontrivial moving-billiard class.
- Major 1 — projective consistency does not cover the linked resolution tuple. The master datum includes `(N_tree,r,N_PPE,N_time,m,n,L,xi,P)` and admissible central calls require `N_time=max{m,n}`, but the formal consistency clause compares data differing only in `(m,n,xi,P)`. Changing `(m,n)` generally forces `N_time` and potentially `r,N_PPE,L` to change, so genuinely admissible calls can fall outside the quantified comparison. As written, independently chosen section kernels such as `q_N=delta_{a_N}` are not formally excluded even though the prose intends a single occurrence kernel frozen before time/mode selection. Required repair: define a datum-independent base incidence kernel; make every resolution/test coordinate a Borel filter/map on it; state invariance of all occurrence records across changes of the entire linked tuple.
- Major 2 — record fields are not formally tied to the active handler, so carrier cost can be omitted. The propagated envelope charges `C_car` only when the recorded passage field satisfies `pi(a)=J`, while the main/nonmain filters are merely named with superscripts `(kappa,pi)` and are not explicitly constrained to the corresponding record-field sets. Thus a mark recorded as `TV` can, under the literal statement, be routed through a `J` main filter without paying `C_car`, invalidating the phase-carrier majorant. Required repair: write the filter subset/equality constraints explicitly; require `G_main` to be a `J` passage; link word/deep ownership to the active handler record; and, if rerouting is allowed, charge `q` by the active handler rather than the stale recorded passage.
- The fresh audit conclusion supersedes the earlier internal claim that v44 had no remaining Major theorem-call gaps. No source or frozen artifact was modified during this audit.
